questions.question: What is S3 Object Lock and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: S3 Object Lock prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a fixed time period or indefinitely. It solves the problem of accidental or malicious deletion of critical data — whether from developer mistakes, ransomware attacks, or internal misuse. It is commonly used for financial records, healthcare data, audit logs, and any data subject to regulatory retention requirements.

questions.question: What is the mandatory prerequisite for enabling S3 Object Lock?
questions.answer: Versioning must be enabled on the bucket before Object Lock can be activated. Object Lock only works on versioning-enabled buckets — this is a hard requirement. When you enable Object Lock during bucket creation, versioning is automatically enabled.

questions.question: What is the difference between Governance Mode and Compliance Mode in Object Lock?
questions.answer: Governance Mode protects objects from deletion, but authorised users with special IAM permissions (like root user) can still overwrite or modify the object. It offers flexibility for internal team scenarios. Compliance Mode is absolute — nobody can delete or modify the locked object during the retention period, not even the root user or AWS itself. It is used for strict regulatory compliance where no exceptions are permitted.

questions.question: What does WORM stand for and how does Object Lock implement it?
questions.answer: WORM stands for Write Once, Read Many. Object Lock implements this by allowing an object to be written to S3 once, after which it can be read any number of times but cannot be overwritten or deleted during the locked period. This turns S3 into an immutable storage system for the locked object.

questions.question: What is SSE-S3 and when is it appropriate to use?
questions.answer: SSE-S3 is Server-Side Encryption with S3 Managed Keys — the default encryption applied to all new S3 objects. AWS S3 automatically manages all encryption keys using AES-256. It is appropriate for most non-sensitive workloads, development environments, or any scenario where you do not need fine-grained control over who can use the encryption key. It is free and requires zero configuration.

questions.question: What is SSE-KMS and why is it preferred in production over SSE-S3?
questions.answer: SSE-KMS is Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS keys. Every KMS operation is logged in AWS CloudTrail — giving you a complete audit trail of who accessed what and when. You control key policies (which IAM users/roles can encrypt/decrypt), set key rotation schedules, and can revoke key access instantly. SSE-S3 provides no audit trail and no key-level access control. For regulated industries (finance, healthcare), this auditability and control is non-negotiable.

questions.question: What is a DEK (Data Encryption Key) and how does it relate to KMS?
questions.answer: A DEK (Data Encryption Key) is a temporary cryptographic key generated by KMS from your master key. In SSE-KMS, S3 does not directly use your KMS master key to encrypt data — because the master key is stored inside a tamper-proof HSM and cannot be extracted. Instead, KMS generates a DEK, S3 uses the DEK to encrypt the actual object data, and the encrypted DEK is stored alongside the encrypted object. On retrieval, S3 sends the encrypted DEK to KMS for decryption, then uses the resulting DEK to decrypt the object.

questions.question: What is an S3 Bucket Key and how does it reduce costs?
questions.answer: S3 Bucket Key is an optimisation for SSE-KMS that reduces KMS API calls. Without it, every object upload and download triggers a separate KMS call, which is charged per call. With Bucket Key, S3 makes one KMS call to generate a long-lived bucket-level DEK, then reuses it for many objects — reducing KMS API calls and costs by up to 99%. The same security level is maintained because the bucket key is still derived from your KMS master key.

questions.question: What is the difference between server-side encryption and client-side encryption in S3?
questions.answer: Server-side encryption (SSE) means you upload data normally and AWS encrypts it on arrival at S3 servers before storing. AWS handles all encryption/decryption transparently when you upload or download. Client-side encryption means you encrypt the data yourself on your own machine before uploading. S3 receives and stores the pre-encrypted blob and never sees your plaintext. Client-side gives maximum control but requires managing encryption logic yourself.

questions.question: What is an S3 lifecycle rule and what are its two types of actions?
questions.answer: An S3 lifecycle rule is an automated policy that manages objects based on age. It has two action types: (1) Transition actions — move objects to a cheaper storage class after a specified number of days (e.g., Standard → Standard-IA after 30 days → Glacier after 90 days); (2) Expiration actions — permanently delete objects after a specified number of days. Lifecycle rules can be scoped to an entire bucket, specific prefixes (folders), or objects with specific tags.

questions.question: Tell me about a situation where you would use CRR vs SRR.
questions.answer: (Situation) We had a production application in Mumbai with no disaster recovery strategy — a regional outage would cause complete data loss. (Task) I needed to implement a replication strategy for business continuity and also consolidate access logs from multiple buckets. (Action) I implemented CRR from Mumbai to Singapore for the production data bucket to ensure disaster recovery across geographic regions. For the application's log buckets spread across the same region, I implemented SRR to consolidate all logs into a single analytics bucket without incurring inter-region transfer costs. (Result) We achieved RTO/RPO compliance for disaster recovery and simplified our log pipeline significantly.

questions.question: A developer reports they cannot upload files to an S3 bucket — they get an Access Denied error. How do you investigate?
questions.answer: (Situation) Upload failures with Access Denied suggest a policy issue rather than a permissions issue at the IAM role level. (Task) Identify and resolve the upload block. (Action) First I would check the bucket policy for any explicit Deny statements. A common scenario is a Deny condition requiring a specific KMS key ARN format — if the upload does not include the correct KMS key reference, the policy blocks it. I would check the error details in CloudTrail, identify the exact condition that triggered the Deny, then either update the developer's upload parameters to include the required KMS key ARN, or consult with the security team to confirm the developer has the correct KMS key access. (Result) The upload succeeds once the correct KMS key ARN is included in the upload request.

questions.question: Your company needs to host a static website on S3 with a custom domain and HTTPS. Walk me through the architecture.
questions.answer: (Situation) S3 static website hosting only supports HTTP natively — we need CloudFront for HTTPS and custom domain support. (Task) Build a production-grade static website serving infrastructure. (Action) Upload website files (HTML/CSS/JS) to an S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled. Keep the bucket private (do not add public bucket policy directly). Create a CloudFront distribution pointing to the S3 bucket as the origin, using Origin Access Control (OAC) so only CloudFront can read from S3. Request a free SSL/TLS certificate from ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) in us-east-1 (required for CloudFront). Attach the ACM certificate to the CloudFront distribution. In Route53, create an A record or ALIAS record pointing your custom domain to the CloudFront distribution. (Result) Users access https://www.mysite.com → Route53 resolves to CloudFront → CloudFront serves cached content over HTTPS from S3.

questions.question: You need to implement a 7-year data retention policy on a financial records S3 bucket where even senior engineers cannot delete files. How do you implement this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Financial regulations require 7-year immutable retention with no exceptions — not even administrative overrides. (Task) Implement technical controls that enforce this retention period absolutely. (Action) Create a new S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled (must be done at creation time) — versioning is automatically enabled. Configure default retention settings on the bucket: set mode to Compliance and retention period to 7 years. Upload all financial records to this bucket. When objects are uploaded, they automatically inherit the default Compliance Mode retention. Any attempt to delete an object during the 7 years will be rejected — by the system — with no override possible. (Result) The bucket technically enforces the retention requirement regardless of who attempts a deletion, satisfying regulatory audits.

questions.question: Your S3 costs are very high because you have 10 million objects encrypted with SSE-KMS. KMS charges are making up 40% of your total AWS bill. How do you reduce this?
questions.answer: (Situation) SSE-KMS normally makes one KMS API call per object upload and download — 10 million objects means potentially millions of daily KMS calls. (Task) Reduce KMS costs without changing the security model. (Action) Enable S3 Bucket Key on the bucket. This changes S3's behaviour so it makes a single KMS call to generate a bucket-level DEK, then reuses it for many objects rather than calling KMS per-object. The security level is unchanged — the bucket key is still derived from and protected by the KMS master key. (Result) KMS API calls dropped by approximately 99%, reducing KMS charges from 40% of the bill to under 1%.

questions.question: You set up CRR from bucket-A (Mumbai) to bucket-B (Singapore). After enabling replication, you notice that objects uploaded before the replication rule was created are missing from bucket-B. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) S3 Replication only replicates new objects uploaded after the replication rule is created — existing objects are not automatically backfilled. (Task) Replicate the existing 500,000 objects to the destination. (Action) Use S3 Batch Replication — this is a separate feature designed specifically to backfill existing objects from source to destination. Go to S3 → Batch Operations → Create job → choose Replicate as the operation → specify the manifest (list of objects) or let it auto-discover all objects in the source bucket → run the job. (Result) All existing objects are replicated to bucket-B. Going forward, both new and existing objects are in sync.

questions.question: Your company stores 5 years of customer data in S3 Standard. The data is accessed frequently in the first month, occasionally in months 2-6, and rarely after 6 months. Design the lifecycle rules.
questions.answer: (Situation) Keeping all data in S3 Standard is expensive for data that is rarely accessed after 6 months. (Task) Design lifecycle rules to optimise storage costs while maintaining appropriate access speeds. (Action) Create a lifecycle rule with three actions: Transition to S3 Standard-IA at 30 days (data is still occasionally needed at a lower access frequency, Standard-IA costs ~58% less than Standard but has a retrieval fee). Transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 180 days (data is rarely accessed, retrieval in hours is acceptable, 85% cheaper than Standard). No expiration since the data must be retained for 5 years. (Result) Storage costs optimised significantly — only the hot first-30-day data pays Standard rates.

questions.question: What would happen to your KMS encrypted objects if you accidentally delete your Customer Managed Key in KMS?
questions.answer: (Situation) Deleting a KMS key is irreversible — AWS gives a 7–30 day waiting period before final deletion as a safety measure. (Task) Understanding the impact. (Action/Answer) If the CMK is deleted, all objects encrypted with that key become permanently undecryptable — you will never be able to access them again, even with AWS support. AWS cannot recover deleted key material since it is destroyed in the HSM. This is why best practices recommend: (1) enabling key deletion protection where possible, (2) scheduling deletion with the maximum 30-day waiting period to allow time to cancel, (3) monitoring CloudTrail for any key scheduling events, and (4) testing restoration procedures before relying on a key for critical data.

questions.question: What is key rotation and why is it important in KMS?
questions.answer: Key rotation is the practice of automatically replacing the active cryptographic key with a new one on a scheduled basis (typically annually for AWS Managed Keys, or 90 days to custom periods for Customer Managed Keys). It is important because: (1) if a key is somehow compromised, rotation limits the window of exposure, (2) regulatory frameworks often mandate key rotation as part of key management best practices, (3) it reduces the risk of cryptanalysis attacks that become more viable the longer the same key is used. Importantly, AWS KMS retains all old key versions, so existing objects encrypted with older key versions can still be decrypted — objects do not need to be re-encrypted after rotation.

questions.question: How would you enforce that only objects encrypted with a specific KMS key can be uploaded to a production S3 bucket?
questions.answer: (Situation) In regulated environments, you need to ensure all uploaded objects use an approved KMS key — not SSE-S3 or unintended keys. (Task) Enforce this via bucket policy. (Action) Add a Deny statement to the bucket policy that blocks s3:PutObject requests where the encryption header does not reference the specific KMS Key ARN. The condition checks that the x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id header matches the approved key ARN in the format arn:aws:kms:region:account-id:key/key-id. Any upload that omits this header or uses a different key is rejected with Access Denied. (Result) Only uploads using the approved CMK are accepted — accidental uploads with SSE-S3 or no encryption are blocked.

questions.question: Explain the complete SSE-KMS encryption and decryption flow for an S3 object, including the role of DEK and the HSM.
questions.answer: Encryption: (1) User uploads object to an SSE-KMS bucket. (2) S3 calls KMS API with the KMS Key ARN. (3) KMS, operating inside a tamper-proof HSM, generates a Data Encryption Key (DEK) — a temporary symmetric key derived from the master key. (4) KMS returns two copies of the DEK: one plaintext (for S3 to use immediately) and one encrypted (using the master key). (5) S3 uses the plaintext DEK to encrypt the object data. (6) S3 stores the encrypted object alongside the encrypted DEK. The plaintext DEK is immediately discarded and never stored. Decryption: (1) User requests object from S3. (2) S3 sends the encrypted DEK to KMS. (3) KMS decrypts the DEK (inside the HSM) and returns the plaintext DEK to S3. (4) S3 uses the plaintext DEK to decrypt the object and delivers it to the user. (5) The plaintext DEK is discarded again.

questions.question: What is the architectural difference between S3 Transfer Acceleration and S3 Cross-Region Replication? When would you use each?
questions.answer: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads TO S3 from end users worldwide. It routes upload traffic through AWS CloudFront edge locations, which then use AWS's high-speed backbone to forward the data to the S3 bucket's home region. Use it when users worldwide are uploading files to a central S3 bucket and experiencing slow upload speeds. Cross-Region Replication automatically copies objects FROM one S3 bucket TO another bucket in a different region. It is asynchronous and operates on data already in S3. Use it for disaster recovery (copy to a DR region), compliance (data in multiple geographic regions), or reducing read latency (replicate to a region closer to read consumers). Key difference: Transfer Acceleration optimises writes from the public internet to S3; CRR optimises data availability and durability across regions after data is in S3.

questions.question: How does S3 Replication handle delete operations? What are the implications for disaster recovery?
questions.answer: By default, S3 Replication does NOT replicate delete markers. If you delete an object in the source bucket (creating a delete marker), the delete marker is not copied to the destination bucket — the object remains accessible in the destination. This is a deliberate design choice to protect against accidental or malicious deletions propagating to your replica. You can optionally enable 'Replicate delete markers' in the replication rule if you want deletions to propagate. For disaster recovery implications: the default behaviour means your DR replica is protected from delete operations in production — if an attacker or runaway script deletes objects in the source, they survive in the replica. This is generally the desired DR behaviour. However, if you intentionally delete objects (e.g., GDPR erasure requests), you must separately delete them from the replica bucket.

questions.question: Describe how you would architect a multi-region active-active S3 setup where changes in either region are visible to users in both regions with sub-15-minute replication.
questions.answer: Architecture: Set up two S3 buckets in different regions (e.g., Mumbai and Singapore) with versioning enabled on both. Configure bidirectional replication: CRR from Mumbai to Singapore AND a separate CRR rule from Singapore to Mumbai — S3 supports bidirectional replication but you must configure both directions explicitly. Enable S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) on both rules to get the 99.99% within 15 minutes SLA with CloudWatch monitoring. S3 handles replication loop prevention automatically — an object replicated from Mumbai to Singapore will not be re-replicated back to Mumbai. Use Route53 latency-based routing or geolocation routing to direct users to the nearest region. Use CloudFront in each region for read performance. Important consideration: Without an application-level conflict resolution strategy, concurrent writes to the same object key in both regions will result in the 'last writer wins' based on replication timing — design your application to avoid conflicting writes or implement conflict resolution logic.

questions.question: You are doing a security review of an S3 architecture. What are the five most critical S3 security controls you would verify?
questions.answer: (1) Block Public Access: Confirm it is enabled at account and bucket level unless there is a specific justified reason for public access (like a static website bucket). (2) Encryption: Verify SSE-KMS is configured for sensitive buckets with Customer Managed Keys — not SSE-S3 or no encryption — so there is an audit trail and key access control. (3) Bucket Policy and ACLs: Review all bucket policies for overly permissive statements (especially Principal: * with no conditions). Ensure legacy ACLs are disabled in favour of bucket policies. (4) Versioning and Object Lock: Check that critical data buckets have versioning enabled as protection against accidental deletion, and Object Lock (Compliance Mode) for any data subject to retention regulations. (5) Access Logging and CloudTrail: Confirm S3 access logging is enabled and that CloudTrail is capturing S3 data events — without this, you have no visibility into who accessed or modified objects, making incident investigation impossible.
